name: Resveratrol derivative pterostilbene

lead: Pterostilbene is a plant compound closely related to resveratrol, found in blueberries, almonds and grape leaves. It is better absorbed orally than resveratrol, according to Wikipedia (about 80% versus 20%).
People take it as an antioxidant and "longevity" supplement, sometimes paired with nicotinamide riboside, with the hope of healthier-looking, aging-resistant skin.

paras: It is sold as an oral supplement, alone or combined with NAD+-boosting compounds like nicotinamide riboside. No dosing is given here.
A small study found it safe in healthy adults for 6-8 weeks, while other studies reported higher LDL and lower HDL cholesterol within 4-8 weeks.

angle.text: Supplement users take pterostilbene for antioxidant support, hoping this slows visible aging. Trials have focused on other outcomes.

lead: Pterostilbene is a stilbenoid in blueberries, almonds and grape vines, differing from resveratrol by two methoxy groups.[1] Plants make it from resveratrol.[1]
Its greater lipophilicity improves oral absorption relative to resveratrol.[1]
Human trials examine it mostly with nicotinamide riboside (NRPT) for muscle, liver and kidney outcomes.[2][3][4]

paras: Wikipedia reports roughly 80% oral bioavailability versus about 20% for resveratrol, attributed to its methoxy groups.[1]
A small study found 250 mg daily for 6-8 weeks safe in healthy adults; other studies reported raised LDL and lowered HDL cholesterol within 4-8 weeks.[1]

Randomized trials of nicotinamide riboside plus pterostilbene have looked at muscle injury in older adults and hepatic inflammation in fatty liver disease.[2][3] A review summarizes biomedical applications of pterostilbene.[5] No studies found examining skin appearance.
